title: Thanksgiving
hook: in North America, a harvest thanks at the table

segments.voice: Yesterday, Servant king: a crown of thorns, and a kingdom not of this world. Your line was a different king. What small job did you do on purpose? Day one thousand fifty-nine.

The ship has been driven by a storm for fourteen days. No sun, no stars. The cargo has gone over the side. The sailors have just been caught trying to slip away in the lifeboat. It's the dark before dawn, and nobody aboard has eaten properly since the storm began. Then one prisoner, a tentmaker called Paul, speaks up in the middle of it, takes a loaf of bread, and does something completely ordinary. He says grace. A strange place to begin a day about Thanksgiving, the holiday when, in North America, families sit down to a harvest meal and give thanks at the table. But that storm is where today starts. Today's word: Thanksgiving.

Here is Acts, in the King James words. Paul urges them all to eat, and then "he took bread, and gave thanks to God in presence of them all: and when he had broken it, he began to eat." Notice what he doesn't wait for. The storm isn't over. The ship hasn't reached land. He gives thanks in the middle, in front of terrified people, and the next verse says: "Then were they all of good cheer, and they also took some meat." One person's grace turned into everyone's breakfast. Paul's grace has a pattern behind it. In Mark's Gospel, with a hungry crowd in the wilderness, Jesus takes the loaves, gives thanks, breaks them, and gives them to his disciples to set before the people. In Luke, two friends at Emmaus only recognize the risen Jesus when he takes bread, blesses it and breaks it. More than once in the Gospels, the meal begins with thanks. A letter in Paul's name puts the idea plainly: "For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving." Creature there means every created thing. The potatoes count. And to the church at Thessalonica, Paul wrote: "In every thing give thanks." Not for every thing, some readers point out. In every thing. In the storm, too. So at a Thanksgiving table, when someone says grace over a harvest meal, the words change from house to house. Some use the Psalms: "O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever." Some say a grace their grandmother said. Some just hold hands for a moment. The shape is the same as on that ship: stop, give thanks out loud, then eat together.
screen: `JESUS TOOK THE LOAVES AND GAVE THANKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say grace before a meal, or get ready to. Settle, and breathe. Think of the next meal you'll eat, and where you'll be. Then think of one thing in your life that isn't settled yet, a storm still going. Don't try to solve it. Just let it be there, the way the storm was there for Paul. Now choose a few plain words of thanks you could say before that meal anyway. If you pray, you can use a grace your family knows, or the psalm's line: O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good. If you don't, just choose the words, and the breath you'll pause for before you eat. The bell holds the time.
Thanksgiving. In North America, a harvest meal with thanks at the table. In the Bible, giving thanks in every thing, even in the middle of a storm.

Your line: for all good gifts. Before your next meal, stop for one breath and give thanks out loud, even if something in your day is still unsettled, the way Paul did on the ship. Day one thousand fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Some Christian families in the United States and Canada say grace before the Thanksgiving meal, sometimes holding hands, and some churches hold a Thanksgiving service or gather food for neighbors in need.

take bread, give thanks in front of everyone, and eat.

trapdoor: what you thought: a holiday about turkey and family.
what it means: a harvest meal begun with thanks at the table, the same shape as Paul's grace in the storm.
what a scholar hears: in every thing give thanks, not for every thing. the thanks comes in the storm, before it's over.

notes: Claims rule: no dates or origin story for Thanksgiving (1621, Lincoln's proclamation, Canada's October date) are given; the index hook supplies 'in North America, a harvest thanks at the table'.
Consider whether a brief, careful word belongs here about Native American experience of the holiday; left out of the voice as outside the cited text.

'Fourteen days' is Acts 27:33 ('the fourteenth day'); 'no sun, no stars' is Acts 27:20; cargo and tackle thrown out 27:18–19; sailors and the boat 27:30–32. Confirm the sequence and 'the dark before dawn' (27:33, 'while the day was coming on').
1 Timothy is described as 'a letter in Paul's name' to avoid an authorship claim. Confirm the Keeper is comfortable with this phrasing.
'Not for every thing, some readers point out. In every thing.' is now attributed to some readers.
'Creature there means every created thing' is a gloss on the KJV word. Confirm.
Carry 'for all good gifts' echoes day 1049 ('all good gifts'); the angle here is grace at the table, in an unsettled moment, rather than harvest produce.

Editor pass: the feeding scene moved from John 6 (the boy's loaves, used tomorrow for Andrew) to Mark 8:6, and the original word now cites Mark 8:6; 'Paul wasn't inventing anything. He was copying' (a claim about his intent) became 'Paul's grace has a pattern behind it'; 'again and again' softened to 'more than once'; the practice and carry no longer trace food back to the people who grew it (day 1049's practice) and instead give thanks in the middle of something unsettled, as Paul did.

Second editor pass: fork setup 'no food' changed to 'almost nobody has eaten' (Acts 27:33 says they had been fasting; 27:38 shows wheat still aboard); the stock line 'they're standing in a long line' cut, also to avoid anticipating day 1061's line image.

Audit pass: Paul 'stands up' (Acts 27:21, earlier speech) changed to 'speaks up' for the grace at 27:33–35; Mark 8:6 now says Jesus gave the loaves to his disciples to set before the people (not that he handed them out), in the teach, match and original note; the word segment no longer reduces thanksgiving to Paul's one grace.
